newsitem.title: DENMARK: Danish court to set rules for historic EU battle.
newsitem.headline: Danish court to set rules for historic EU battle.

text.p: A court is to mark out the field of battle on Friday for a constitutional fight that legal experts say could force Denmark out of the European Union or into an unplanned general election.

A non-partisan group of 11 Danes has filed suit against the government, saying their country's ratification of EU treaties could contravene a clause in the constitution limiting how much national sovereignty may be ceded abroad.

Friday's hearing must decide if the challengers' case should be limited to the EU's 1992 Maastricht accord, as government lawyers will argue, or if it should extend to the more comprehensive Treaty of Rome on which the bloc was founded.
"The Maastricht treaty itself does not transfer that much in sovereignty," Hjalte Rasmussen, professor of European law at Copenhagen University, told Reuters.
"The government has taken the view that it will only respond to the very narrow Maastricht transfer," he said.
If the court decided to test the Treaty of Rome the prospect of a win for the petitioners could increase, he said.

Christian Harlang, lawyer for the 11, says the hearings and an inevitable Supreme Court appeal by whoever loses the final district court verdict are likely to run into the autumn of 1998 at the earliest.
But the outcome will to a large extent be determined at Friday's pre-trial session, Harlang added.
"We are very excited, because if the government barrister loses on this our chance of success in the substantive trial is much better," he said.
The petitioners will seek to prove that the treaties do not sufficiently define the extent to which the European Court and other EU institutions may override national bodies.
The Danish constitution's Article 20 states that national powers may be be delegated to international bodies only "within a specified limit".
The government is confident that its case is watertight, at least as far as the 1992 accord is concerned.

"Based on years of legal practice, the government is convinced that Denmark's accession to the Maastricht treaty is in accordance with the Danish constitution," Prime Minister Poul Nyrup Rasmussen said last August.

He was speaking the day after the Supreme Court, sitting with a panel of nine judges, surprised Danes and unnerved other EU members by overturning a lower court's refusal to allow the suit, which has been awaiting a hearing since 1993.
"The judgment came as a shock, what just a few days before had been considered an unthinkable situation was suddenly the reality which people had to confront," Hjalte Rasmussen said.

The language of the Supreme Court ruling contains hints that the judges might just be leaning towards the wider interpretation of the petition that could end Denmark's EU membership under present terms.

Traditional judicial reluctance to challenge legislation and the enormous upheaval that would result if the treaties were found to be at odds with the constitution leave most lawyers unable to envisage such a verdict, Hjalte Rasmussen says.
But if the Supreme Court does back the 11, the government would face hard options.

It could amend the constitution so that conflict with the EU treaties was removed. However, to do so it would first have to win a parliamentary vote for change, then dissolve itself and fight a new general election on the issue of the proposed amendment.

One alternative would be to renegotiate Denmark's EU membership. "Denmark could no longer be a member of the European Union," constitutional law professor Henrik Zahle wrote after the August Supreme Court ruling.

Danes have a history of coolness toward the EU. They rejected Maastricht altogether in a 1992 referendum and approved it the following year only on condition that Denmark stay out of European Monetary Union and joint defence, policing and citizenship arrangements.
